subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Brooklands: The First Circuit
description: A quick win: understand Brooklands: The First Circuit.

hook.text: In 1907, a wealthy Englishman built the world's first purpose-built racetrack on his own estate.

buildup.text: Brooklands was a banked concrete oval in Surrey, designed for cars to reach their maximum speed.

discovery.text: Its steep banking let cars carry speed through turns without braking—a revolutionary design idea.

twist.text: The bumpy concrete surface was terrifying at high speed, and crashes were frequent from the start.

climax.text: Brooklands became the birthplace of British motorsport and stood for 32 years until World War II.

punchline.text: One man's backyard became the cradle of racing.

quiz.question: What was special about Brooklands when it opened in 1907?

details.summary: Brooklands, opened in 1907 in Surrey, England, was the world's first purpose-built motor racing circuit, featuring a banked concrete oval that hosted races, speed records, and aircraft testing for decades.
details.whyItMatters: Brooklands established the concept of a permanent racing venue, transforming motorsport from dangerous public road events into organized spectacle and advancing automotive engineering.
takeaways: It opened in 1907 as the first purpose-built racing circuit
The banked concrete oval allowed speeds over 140 mph by the 1930s
It doubled as an aircraft manufacturing and testing facility

faq.question: Is Brooklands still used for racing today?
faq.answer: No. The circuit was requisitioned for aircraft production during World War II and never fully reopened. Parts of the bankings survive and the site now houses the Brooklands Museum and Mercedes-Benz World.

faq.question: Why was a purpose-built circuit necessary?
faq.answer: Racing on public roads was banned in Britain. Brooklands gave racers and manufacturers a legal, controlled venue to test speed and develop cars without endangering the public.
